title: Immutability
body:
Once a value is built it never changes. [[Haskell]] has no assignment operator: `x = 5` binds a
name to a value permanently, and `x = x + 1` is an equation with no solution rather than an
increment. You do not have variables in the [[Variable|C sense]] of a named box you can write
into; you have names for values.

Updating means **building a new value that shares most of its parts with the old one**:

```haskell
xs = [1, 2, 3]
ys = 0 : xs        -- ys is [0,1,2,3]; xs is still [1,2,3] and was not copied
```

`ys` holds a new cell whose tail *points at* `xs`. Both lists are usable, neither can be
corrupted by the other, and the operation is $O(1)$. Structures that work this way are called
**persistent**: the old version survives every update.

Sharing is safe only because nothing is mutable. In [[C]] two [[Pointer|pointers]] into one
structure is a hazard you have to track by hand; here it is the default and costs nothing,
because there is no write that could surprise the other holder.

## What it costs

Not everything is $O(1)$. Updating the middle of a list rebuilds the spine down to that point,
and there is no way to write one element of an [[Array]] in place, which is why array-heavy
algorithms ([[Quick Sort]] partitioning, [[Hashing|hash table]] probing) are genuinely awkward
in a pure language and get special support rather than a naive translation. The general shape:
immutability is cheap for structures you extend at one end and expensive for structures you
poke at random.

## Why it is the concurrency argument

This is where the paradigm stops being taste. A race requires two things at once: shared data,
and at least one writer. Immutable data has no writer, so the race is not prevented, it is
**unrepresentable**, and there is no [[Critical Section]] to identify in the first place.

| | mutable | immutable |
|---|---|---|
| Two [[Thread\|threads]] read | safe | safe |
| One writes, one reads | race; needs a [[Mutex Lock]] | cannot arise |
| Passing data to another thread | copy, or lock and hope | pass the pointer, always safe |

Every lock note in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] ([[Mutex Lock]], [[Spin Lock]], [[Semaphores]],
[[Synchronization]]) exists to serialise access to shared mutable state. Remove the mutability
and the whole apparatus has nothing to do. That is the same argument [[Pure Function]] makes
about code; this is the data half of it.

The idea has leaked well beyond functional languages: `final` in [[Java]], `const` in [[C]],
`Object.freeze` and the "never mutate state directly" rule in [[React]] are all the same
observation reached from the imperative side.

## Core Facts to Know

- Names bind to values once; there is no assignment and no mutation.
- `x = x + 1` is an equation with no solution, not an increment.
- Update means building a new value that **shares** structure with the old one.
- Structures where the old version survives an update are **persistent**.
- Sharing is free and safe precisely because nothing can be written.
- Cheap at the ends, expensive in the middle: no in-place array update.
- A race needs shared data *and* a writer, so immutable data cannot race.
- It makes locks unnecessary rather than easier.
- `final`, `const`, and [[React]]'s state rule are the same idea in imperative languages.
